name: Fiano

lines.s10: Fiano is the waxy, nutty white of Campania's high hills: ripe pear, honeysuckle and toasted hazelnut, with real weight.
lines.s20: Fiano belongs to Irpinia, the cool hills around Avellino, inland from Naples. It is a dry white with body and a waxy feel, and it tastes of ripe pear, honeysuckle and hazelnut, turning to honey and toast with age.
lines.s45: Fiano is a southern white that behaves like a northern one. Its home is Irpinia, the cool, high hills inland from Naples. It tastes of ripe pear, honeysuckle and toasted hazelnut, with a trace of smoke. It is dry, medium to full in body and a little waxy, with fresh acidity. Most ferments in steel and rests on its yeast for texture, and it keeps: in ten years it turns to honey and toast. It has the weight for roast chicken, mushroom pasta or buffalo mozzarella. The Romans are said to have named it for the bees its sweet grapes drew, and the label may still say Apianum.
lines.sale: Fiano carries a main course without any help from new oak: ripe pear, hazelnut and a trace of smoke. I would serve it cool but not ice cold, with the roast chicken or a mushroom pasta.

glass.lead: Ripe pear and honeysuckle over toasted hazelnut and a trace of smoke, dry, waxy and medium to full in body.

ladder.where: The high hills of Irpinia, around Avellino
The Campanian coast, Puglia, Sicily and McLaren Vale

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium plus and fresh, alcohol moderate to medium plus, body medium to full, with a waxy, faintly oily texture.

home.home: Irpinia, the high hills around Avellino in Campania, 400 to 700 metres up, with cold winters and an October harvest. Fiano di Avellino must be at least 85 per cent Fiano, from twenty-six communes. It is made mostly in steel and rested on its lees, a little in used oak, and it gains honey and toast over a decade.
home.abroad: Elsewhere in the south of Italy it grows on the Campanian coast, in Puglia and in Sicily, with riper fruit. In Australia it has found a second home in McLaren Vale, where it keeps its acidity in the heat.

service.temp: 50 to 55 degrees Fahrenheit, 10 to 13 degrees Celsius: cellar cool, not ice cold.
service.glass: A white wine glass; a wider bowl for an older bottle.
service.decant: Rarely. A mature or tightly wound bottle can open with a little air; taste a sample first.
service.age: Good young, and a white that keeps: Fiano di Avellino can gain honey and toast over ten years.

A separate, muscat scented grape of Puglia, properly Minutolo, despite the shared name.

guest.q: Is this a light white or a rich one?
guest.a: Between the two, and nearer rich. Fiano has body and a waxy feel, with ripe pear, honeysuckle and hazelnut, but it has fresh acidity and no new oak, so it does not feel heavy.

guest.q: I taste nuts and a little smoke. Is there oak in this?
guest.a: Usually none, or only old casks. The hazelnut and the trace of smoke belong to the grape and its hills, and they deepen as the wine ages.

guest.q: Can a white from so far south really be fresh?
guest.a: Yes. The vineyards sit high in the hills inland from Naples, where the nights are cold and the harvest is late, so the wine keeps its acidity.

compare.tell: Chardonnay without oak is cleaner and more neutral, with lemon and green apple; Fiano is waxier and more scented, with honeysuckle, hazelnut and a trace of smoke.
Verdicchio is leaner and sharper, with lemon, green almond and a bitter finish; Fiano is broader and waxier, with ripe pear and hazelnut.
Vermentino is lighter and saltier, with lime and wild fennel; Fiano has more body and a waxy feel, with hazelnut and honey.

profile.st: Pale to medium lemon · Body medium to full · Acid medium plus · Alcohol moderate to medium plus · Dry, waxy in texture
profile.fruit: Ripe pear, yellow apple; apricot, nectarine and melon from the coast, Puglia, Sicily and McLaren Vale
profile.other: Honeysuckle and acacia blossom, toasted hazelnut and almond, a trace of smoke; acacia honey, beeswax and toast with age; usually no new oak
profile.tell: A dry southern Italian white with weight and a waxy feel, pear and honeysuckle over hazelnut and smoke, yet fresh in acidity: Fiano di Avellino
profile.regions: Fiano di Avellino and Irpinia in Campania; the Campanian coast, Puglia and Sicily; McLaren Vale in Australia
profile.confuse: Greco di Tufo is tauter, sharper and flintier; Chardonnay without oak is more neutral; Verdicchio is leaner, with a bitter almond finish; Fiano Minutolo is a separate, muscat scented grape

cards.front: Fiano: where is it at home, and what are the rules?
cards.back: Irpinia in Campania. Fiano di Avellino, a DOCG since 2003, is at least 85 per cent Fiano from twenty-six communes around Avellino.

cards.front: What does Apianum on a label of Fiano di Avellino mean?
cards.back: It is the wine's Latin name, from apis, the bee: the grape's sweetness is said to have drawn bees. The rules allow it on the label.

cards.front: Fiano blind against Greco di Tufo, its neighbour: what parts them?
cards.back: Fiano is waxy and nutty, with pear, honeysuckle, hazelnut and weight. Greco di Tufo is tauter and higher in acidity, with bitter almond and a flinty edge.

questions.q: A blind Italian white is dry and medium to full in body, waxy in feel, with ripe pear, honeysuckle, toasted hazelnut and a trace of smoke, fresh acidity and no new oak. Which wine is it most likely to be?
questions.exp: Weight, a waxy feel, hazelnut and smoke point to Fiano from Irpinia. Gavi and Pinot Grigio are lighter and leaner, and Soave is softer, with white peach and bitter almond.

questions.q: A guest sees the word Apianum on a bottle from Campania and asks which grape it points to. What do you answer?
questions.exp: Apianum is the Latin name allowed on Fiano di Avellino, from the word for bee. Greco di Tufo and Falanghina del Sannio are Campania's other white names and carry no such term.

questions.q: A guest wants a white with enough body for roast chicken and mushrooms but dislikes the taste of new oak. Which bottle do you suggest?
questions.exp: Fiano di Avellino takes its weight and waxy texture from the grape, usually with no new oak. Meursault, Napa Chardonnay and white Rioja Reserva are typically raised in barrel.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it. A doubt for the reviewer: the Codex's own McLaren Vale record lists McLaren Vale Fiano among that region's wines and calls the grape a regional signature white there, so a guest can meet a New World style on a list. The entry gives McLaren Vale under abroad; if the plan moves Fiano to the side by side, the two sides are Irpinia and McLaren Vale.

A new grape: the profile is written in the manner of GRAPES, and the six targets are Campania, Puglia, McLaren Vale and Italy (whose records already name Fiano), with Sicily and Australia, which the entry supports.

No Codex record is contradicted. The Codex already holds Fiano di Avellino as a DOCG since 2003, at least 85 per cent Fiano from twenty-six communes, Apianum from the bee, waxy, hazelnut, honeysuckle, pear and smoke with fresh acidity and weight, honey and toast over a decade, steel and lees with some used oak, Irpinia at 400 to 700 metres with cold winters, service at cellar temperature with roast chicken, mushroom pasta or buffalo mozzarella, Fiano in the Salento, Minutolo as a separate grape, and McLaren Vale Fiano keeping its acidity in heat.
Apianum: the tie to a Roman wine and to the bees is tradition and is given as what is said. Whether the Roman vine was this grape is disputed, and Pliny is not named.
Yellow apple, acacia blossom, struck flint, acacia honey and beeswax are a taster's naming around the notes the Codex gives; beeswax and acacia honey in mature wines have a second source.
The Riserva (at least a year) stands on the production rules, which carry a Riserva, and on one reference page for the length; it is given as at least a year and no more.

The ladder: Irpinia is called cool because the Codex's Campania record calls it high, wet and cold for the south; the warm rung is the coast, Puglia, Sicily and McLaren Vale. Riper fruit there is the common account, and the notes on that rung are a taster's reading.

Left out for want of a second source: the grape's decline through the twentieth century and why, small berries and low yields, the month of harvest, the hazelnut groves of Avellino as the cause of the note, and which house planted the grape first in Australia.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.

checked.verdict: Sound after five fixes. Fiano di Avellino at 85 per cent from twenty-six communes, the Riserva added in 2020 at twelve months, the October harvest, honey and nuts with age, riper and fuller fruit from Puglia and Sicily and McLaren Vale holding its acidity in the heat were confirmed.
changed: glass.notes, nutty: bitter almond now reads almond. The entry's third card, its confuse line and its Verdicchio tell all use a bitter almond finish to part Greco di Tufo and Verdicchio from Fiano, as the Codex's reviewed records do, so the entry could not list the note as Fiano's own. Almond is named for Fiano in a page read.

glass.notes, mineral: struck flint now reads wet stone, for the same reason: the Codex gives Greco di Tufo the flinty edge and Fiano the smoke, and the third card repeats it. The trace of smoke stays.

glass.ladder, the warm rung: yellow apple, acacia honey and bitter almond now read apricot, nectarine and honeydew melon. The author gave the rung as a taster's reading. The notes read for the warm sites are apricot and ripe tropical fruit in Sicily, stone fruit in Puglia, and stone fruit, melon and nectarine in McLaren Vale.
profile.fruit: riper and softer from the coast, Puglia and Sicily now names the fruit: apricot, nectarine and melon from the coast, Puglia, Sicily and McLaren Vale.

worlds.home.home: a late harvest now reads an October harvest. Said beside a wine, late harvest reads as a sweet style, and several pages read set the picking in October, late for a white of the south.
open: The plan gives Fiano at home and abroad, and the author's doubt stands for whoever reviews the plan: the Codex's McLaren Vale record calls the grape a regional signature white, and the notes read describe a recognised style there (medium bodied, a little waxy, nectarine and melon, fresh acidity). The mode is left as the plan fixes it.
Honeydew melon names the melon of the McLaren Vale notes, which do not say which melon.
Flint is said of Fiano di Avellino by many tasters and is not wrong of it. It is left to Greco di Tufo here because the Codex teaches the pair that way.
The Riserva at twelve months stands on a reference page and on a second that says an added year; the decree of 13 October 2020 was not opened.
